catalog_citation: Westrum, Peter N. and Susan Westrum. 1975. A preliminary Berik phonology. Irian: Bulletin of Irian Jaya Development 4(1): 1-37.
catalog_locator: Sec. 4 'The Phonological Word', p. 29 (right-hand page of PDF p. 17 of the 2-up issue scan); sec. 4.2 'Compound Words' and 4.3 'Word Repetit…
catalog_quote: The phonological word in Berik is a sequence of one to four syllables with one primary stress always occurring word initially except in the case of word initial /e/ followed by /e/ in which case the stress falls on the second syllable. Since stress is predictable, it is non-phonemic and has not been written other than in the phonetic transcription. /gu/ ['gu] 'cassowary' /amkom/ ['am.kom] 'almost' /sarbasɩn/ ['sar̃.ba.sɩn] 'hear' /fongalabar/ ['foŋ.ga.la.bar̃] 'when' /eebali/ [e'ɛbʌli] 'do' Compound words may have more than four syllables and more than one stress. See Section 4.2.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Held file (Irian 4(1), 1975; Wayback copy of the papuaweb scan; image-only, 37 PDF pages, 2-up spreads). I rendered PDF p. 17 (print pp. 28-29) at 150 dpi and read it directly: section '4 THE PHONOLOGICAL WORD' on p. 29 reads exactly as quoted -- 'The phonological word in Berik is a sequence of one to four syllables with one primary stress always occurring word initially except in the case of word initial /e/ followed by /e/ in which case the stress falls on the second syllable. Since stress is predictable, it is non-phonemic and has not been written other than in the phonetic transcription.' followed by the examples ['gu] 'cassowary', ['am.kom] 'almost', ['sar.ba.sin] 'hear', ['fon.ga.la.b…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the first syllable of the (simple) phonological word; the only stated exception is words beginning in /e.e/ (two successive /e/ syllables), where stress falls on the second syllable. Stress is predictable and non-contrastive.
new_statements.secondary_stress: p. 33, sec. 4.2: 'Compound words... have three, four, or five syllables. The primary stress often occurs on the first syllable and a secondary stress occurs on the first syllable of the second part of the compound. In some cases there is primary stress on the first syllable of the second part of the compound.' e.g. /o.re.le.sa.fa/ ['o.ře.ˌle.'sa.fa] 'beard', /nu.e.tι.fιn/ [nu.e.'tι.fιn] 'eyelid'. Sec. 4.3: in word/syllable repetition the initial syllable of the repeated part receives the same stress as the word-initial syllable, e.g. ['wækεn'wækεnsusu] 'best'.
new_statements.exceptions: Word-initial /e/ followed by /e/ -> stress on second syllable (e.g. /eebali/ [e'ɛbʌli] 'do'); compounds may carry primary stress on the second member instead; Indonesian abstract hedges 'hampir selalu' (almost always) on the first syllable.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the phonological word (1-4 syllables), illustrated with citation forms including suffixed verbs; compounds and reduplications treated separately with their own stress on each member. Based on fieldwork in Tenwer village, Tor River, 1973-74.
new_statements.identity_note: Source describes Berik as spoken in Tenwer (and Somanente) villages on the Tor River, Jayapura regency; this is the language-level beri1254 itself, no dialect split named.

sources.note: Sec. 4 (p. 29): phonological word = 1-4 syllables with one primary stress always word-initial, except word-initial /e/+/e/ where stress falls on the 2nd syllable; stress predictable, non-phonemic. Sec. 4.2 (p. 33): compounds have primary stress on first syllable and secondary on first syllable of second member (sometimes primary there). Sec. 4.3: reduplicated part gets same stress on its initial syllable. Indonesian abstract (p. 1) repeats: 'tekanan utama hampir selalu pada sukukata pertama'.
